section: News Topic Explorer > Why it matters
text: Newsrooms, comms teams and analysts all face the same problem: thousands of headlines a day and no time to read them. A topic model can sort them, but a table of 283 keyword lists is not an answer anyone can act on. This explorer presents the model the way a consultant would present a topic analysis: One question, answered top down. The first screen shows the share of coverage each theme gets. Every click goes one level deeper until you reach real headlines. Honest numbers. Unassigned stories (40% of this corpus) and blank rows are shown, counted and explained instead of hidden. Time aware. News moves by the hour, so every selection comes with its trend, its source mix and a rising and fading view. Human labels.

Read only by design. The app never fits or retrains anything. CacheBuilder reads the pipeline's CSV outputs, the pickled model attributes and the SQLite database (opened with mode=ro), joins them on article id with validate="many_to_one" and writes small parquet tables. The app starts in about two seconds from that cache. A tree that reads well. Raw c-TF-IDF profiles share so few exact words that Ward linkage on them collapses into one long chain. TopicTreeBuilder first projects the profiles onto 30 latent themes (truncated SVD), scales them to unit length so distance follows cosine similarity, then merges with Ward.

the profiles onto 30 latent themes (truncated SVD), scales them to unit length so distance follows cosine similarity, then merges with Ward. The top level went from one branch holding 93% of articles to six balanced themes. Names weighted by size. KeywordNamer combines each topic's keywords, weighted by article count, so larger topics drive the group name. A group never reuses a name from inside its own branch, so breadcrumbs always read as distinct steps. Pluggable data. Pages talk to AbstractDataSource. HeadlineRadarDataSource serves the cache, and FrameDataSource serves in memory tables for tests. A new dataset only needs a new source. Pluggable pages.

A new dataset only needs a new source. Pluggable pages. PortfolioApp registers any list of AbstractPage objects as Dash pages inside one shared AppShell. Project pages come from ProjectRegistry, and the home and projects pages build their cards from the same registry. Fast callbacks. Filters are one boolean mask over 41k rows, branch counts are sums over precomputed topic lists, and a full view renders in about 30 ms. Small, readable classes. One class per file, named after the file. Analytics classes have no Dash imports, so they are easy to test and reuse.

Headline Radar pulls live news headlines from GDELT and seven RSS feeds into a local database, then finds the topics in them with a topic model I wrote from scratch. Every 15 minutes there are thousands of new headlines. Headline Radar groups them into a few hundred readable topics, names each one with keywords, and shows how the topics relate. See the full walkthrough: Topic model notebook How to read this chart: each row on the right is a topic, with its top keywords and its number of articles. Lines join topics that use similar words. The further left two branches meet, the less alike they are, so pairs that join close to the right are the most similar.

The further left two branches meet, the less alike they are, so pairs that join close to the right are the most similar. In this run, the Ukraine and Russia topic sits next to the Gaza and Israel topic, and NFL joins college football (CFP, Notre Dame). The closest pair is crashes and injuries next to police, arrests, and charges. Stock market headlines sit beside Black Friday and iPhone deals. The chart covers 41,277 articles and 283 topics.

Most organizations have more free text than anyone can read. Topic modeling turns that text into a short list of themes you can count, track, and act on. With news, that means you can: Spot new stories and market-moving themes early, as a new topic appears or grows. Track how coverage of a company, sector, or region changes from week to week. Route and triage a large stream of headlines to the right people. The engine does not know anything about news. Point it at any column of short texts and it works the same way. Good fits are support tickets, customer feedback, invoice or claim notes, and survey responses.

I am a Lead Applied AI Scientist. At Signature Aviation I built the enterprise AI platform, covering data engineering, forecasting, dynamic pricing, and MLOps governance. This project shows the same habits on open data. My own BERTopic-style model, not a black box. Sentence embeddings with attention-mask mean pooling, UMAP to reduce them, HDBSCAN to cluster them, and c-TF-IDF to name the topics. Each step is a small, readable method. A loader you can rerun safely. Each article id is the SHA-256 of its URL, so reloads never add duplicates. A watermark per source means each run only pulls new data. Clear handling of edge cases.

A watermark per source means each run only pulls new data. Clear handling of edge cases. Topic -1 means a text did not fit any topic. Topic -2 means the text was blank. The two are never mixed. Honest predictions. For each text, transform_with_status says whether it was in the training data (seen), was predicted (new), or was blank. Safe joins. TopicJoiner adds topic ids to a table without ever adding rows, and it raises an error when the data has drifted from the fitted model. Diagnostics you can check. get_fit_diagnostics shows how cluster sizes changed after identical texts were given one shared topic. The right size of tools.

Diagnostics you can check. get_fit_diagnostics shows how cluster sizes changed after identical texts were given one shared topic. The right size of tools. pandas and SQLite instead of Spark and a database server, because the data fits on one machine. Tested on real data. 41,277 articles became 283 topics, with 40% left as outliers. The full run took about 3.5 minutes on CPU. Some topics pick up publisher boilerplate, such as "targeted news service". The example texts for each topic make those easy to spot and relabel.

TextEmbedder builds sentence embeddings straight from the raw transformer output. It averages token vectors with the attention mask so padding never counts, then scales each vector to length 1. It needs no sentence-transformers package and can save and reload the model for offline use. TopicModel is my own BERTopic-style pipeline: UMAP, HDBSCAN, and class-based TF-IDF. Copies of the same text vote on one shared topic, and topics that shrink below the minimum size after the vote are pruned again. It tells seen texts from new ones, predicts new ones with HDBSCAN approximate_predict, and reports fit diagnostics.

It tells seen texts from new ones, predicts new ones with HDBSCAN approximate_predict, and reports fit diagnostics. TopicHierarchyPlot compares topics by the cosine distance between their c-TF-IDF vectors and links them with Ward linkage. The Plotly dendrogram shows the combined keywords at every merge point when you hover. TopicJoiner joins topic ids back onto a table by exact text. It checks that the join keeps the row count, gives blank text -2, and raises an error on conflicting ids or on text the model has never seen, which is a sign of drift.

TopicExplorer writes one self-contained HTML page: a 2D UMAP map of every unique text colored by topic, a bar chart of topic sizes, and a table of keywords and example texts. It works offline. GdeltLoader and RssLoader share one base class, NewsLoader, that logs every run and advances the watermark only after a successful load. The GDELT loader walks the 15-minute files from the last watermark, saves progress after each file, and retries a file on the next run if it is not published yet.
15-minute files from the last watermark, saves progress after each file, and retries a file on the next run if it is not published yet. Files still missing after a 45-minute grace period are skipped.

models/TopicModel.py works on any list of short texts. Embed each unique text with TextEmbedder (MiniLM). Reduce the embeddings to 5 dimensions with UMAP. Give identical texts the same topic. Move any topic smaller than min_topic_size to the outliers. Number topics by size, so topic 0 is the largest. Describe each topic with c-TF-IDF keywords and three example texts. Texts from the fit data get their fitted topic back. New texts are placed with HDBSCAN approximate_predict. The model only knows the data it was fit on, so refit it as new headlines arrive. TopicJoiner adds a topic_id column to a pandas DataFrame by exact text match.

TopicJoiner adds a topic_id column to a pandas DataFrame by exact text match. It never adds rows and gives blank text -2. It raises an error if one text has two topic ids, or if a text is missing from the lookup, which means the model needs a refit.

data/headline_radar.db is a SQLite file with three tables. The schema lives in utils/storage/Database.py. The tables are linked by the source name (gdelt or rss). These links are by value only. There are no foreign key constraints. No duplicates on reload. articles.id is the SHA-256 of the URL, and inserts use INSERT OR IGNORE, so rerunning a load skips articles that are already stored. Incremental loads. watermarks keeps one high-water mark per source. The next run starts from it and only pulls new data. An audit log.

Incremental loads. watermarks keeps one high-water mark per source. The next run starts from it and only pulls new data. An audit log. load_runs gets one row per run, with its status, counts fetched, inserted, and skipped, the high-water mark it reached, and any error. Blanks stay blank. Missing titles or descriptions are stored as NULL, and the row is kept. Zero setup. SQLite needs no server. Timestamps are stored as UTC text and the SQL is plain, so moving to Postgres later is simple.

GDELT data comes from the 15-minute GKG files advertised by https://data.gdeltproject.org/gdeltv2/lastupdate.txt. Titles are read from the GKG PAGE_TITLE extras field; a precise publish time is used when PAGE_PRECISEPUBTIMESTAMP is present, otherwise the 15-minute file time. GKG does not include article descriptions, so those are stored as NULL. Files are downloaded over HTTPS; the HTTP URLs in lastupdate.txt often return 500. The very newest file listed in lastupdate can 404 for a short time and is retried on the next run.

The very newest file listed in lastupdate can 404 for a short time and is retried on the next run. The GDELT DOC 2.0 API also exposes titles, but it rate-limits to one request every five seconds and, during setup, frequently returned HTTP 429 or an empty JSON object, so it is not used here. RSS feeds included here: BBC News, NPR News, CNBC Top Stories, Guardian Business, MarketWatch, NYT World, and Al Jazeera. Feeds that did not respond during setup (Yahoo Finance 404, Politico 403, CNN SSL error) were left out.
